differential.key_features: MS relapse could produce diplopia and weakness, but MS relapses do not produce fatigable diurnal pattern or RNS decrement; brain MRI does not show new enhancing lesion explaining symptoms.
Patient on natalizumab — PML must be ruled out with MRI (no characteristic lesion here) and CSF JCV PCR if doubt remains.
No malignancy history; high-rate RNS expected to show no facilitation; baseline CMAP normal.
Patient has diplopia rather than monocular visual loss; visual evoked potentials and OCT can clarify.
INO produces specific adduction failure pattern; fatigable bilateral ptosis is incompatible.

key_clinical_evidence: Fluctuating, fatigable weakness with diurnal pattern (worse evening) is the clinical hallmark of MG — fixed weakness suggests an alternative diagnosis.
Ocular involvement (ptosis, diplopia) is asymmetric and fatigable in MG; thyroid eye disease causes restrictive (not fatigable) ophthalmoplegia.
Single-fiber EMG (sensitivity >95%) is the most sensitive electrodiagnostic test — order when RNS is non-diagnostic or serology is negative.
All confirmed MG cases require CT chest for thymoma — present in roughly 10-15% of generalized MG; thymectomy (MGTX trial) improves long-term outcomes in non-thymoma AChR+ MG as well.
Aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones, telithromycin, IV magnesium, and neuromuscular blockers can precipitate myasthenic crisis and must be screened against any new prescription.
MS and MG can coexist (polyautoimmunity) and natalizumab has rare reports of triggering secondary autoimmune disease; clinical pattern (fatigable, fluctuating) distinguishes MG from MS relapse.
Brain MRI is essential here NOT because of MG, but to rule out PML and active MS — case-specific justification for brain MRI in MG workup.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: MS relapses do not produce fatigable diurnal weakness or RNS decrement; AChR antibodies are required to confirm coexisting MG.
red_herrings.intended_effect: Attribute all new neurological symptoms to MS relapse and pursue steroid pulse without considering MG.

patient.chief_complaint: New bilateral ptosis and diplopia attributed to possible MS relapse

past_medical_history: Multiple sclerosis (relapsing-remitting, diagnosed 4 years ago, on natalizumab)

patient.history_present_illness: A 38-year-old woman with relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis on natalizumab presented for evaluation of new bilateral ptosis and diplopia over 6 weeks. She had been referred to the neurology clinic by her MS neurologist for evaluation of possible MS relapse. Her MS neurologist's concern was a new oculomotor finding on top of her prior documented internuclear ophthalmoplegia from an older right MLF lesion. The patient reports the bilateral eyelid drooping began approximately 6 weeks ago, initially intermittent and present mainly in the evenings. She noted double vision — horizontal, worsening on sustained upgaze — that was new and different from her chronic INO-related symptoms. Her MS neurologist had prescribed a 5-day course of high-dose IV methylprednisolone 2 weeks ago for presumed MS relapse. The ptosis and diplopia showed minimal improvement with steroids, which was unexpected for an acute MS relapse. She then began to notice mild fatigue when using her arms for overhead activities (hanging laundry, reaching for shelves) and mild difficulty chewing tough meats. She denied significant dysphagia. Her prior MS symptoms (right-sided hemiparesis, cerebellar ataxia, INO) are all at their chronic stable baseline. Repeat brain MRI performed 1 week ago for relapse evaluation showed no new or enhancing MS lesions. Anti-JC antibody index is elevated at 3.1 (high PML risk — she is on natalizumab extension beyond 24 months). Her MS neurologist noted the poor steroid response and the new neuromuscular features (jaw fatigue, arm fatigue) were atypical for an MS relapse and referred to general neurology for further evaluation. Anti-AChR antibodies have not been checked.
